351.title: Not my contest
351.hook: you can be unbeatable if you enter no contest where winning isn't up to you (Enchiridion 19)
351.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners notice when they start comparing themselves with others and decline to stake their peace on outcomes that depend on others.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the raven croaks. Your line was just a bird. When something felt like a bad sign, did you sort it and let it fly off? Day three hundred fifty-one.

Late at night, thumb on the screen. An old classmate just bought a house. Someone's kid got into the program. A coworker is posting from a beach that looks fake it's so blue. Nobody announced a race. Nobody handed out numbers. And yet somehow you're running, and losing, at eleven forty on a Tuesday. Epictetus never saw a phone, but he lived in a city full of competitions: athletes, orators, men chasing office. Section nineteen of the handbook makes a claim that sounds like a boast. He says you can be unbeatable. Today: not my contest.
screen: `ELEVEN FORTY ON A TUESDAY.` → `A RACE NOBODY ANNOUNCED.` → `YOU CAN BE UNBEATABLE.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. You can be invincible, Epictetus says, if you never enter a contest where winning isn't up to you. The Greek for contest is agon, the word behind the games, the law courts, and in the end our word agony. Second, the trap. When you see someone honored above you, or powerful, or admired, he says, watch out that the impression doesn't carry you off into thinking they must be happy. That's the moment we sign up for a contest without noticing: their house, their title, their beach, and suddenly we're competitors. Third, the reasoning. If what's truly good lies in what's up to us, he says, then there's no room for envy or jealousy. You can't envy someone for something that was never the prize. And then the line: you yourself don't want to be a general or a senator or a consul. You want to be free. And there's only one road to that: to care little for things not in our power. Fourth, what's left. This isn't a refusal to try at anything. Train for the race, apply for the job, write the book. What Epictetus refuses is to stake your peace on the result, which depends on judges, timing and other people. The contest where winning is up to you is a different one: patience against your own temper, honesty against your own excuses. You can win that one every day. Nobody else even has to be in it. So the next time the scrolling starts a race, you can stand at the line, watch the runners go, and say: not my contest.
screen: `AGON: THE CONTEST.` · `DON'T THINK THE HONORED ARE HAPPY.` · `NOT A GENERAL. FREE.` · `THE CONTEST YOU CAN WIN.` · then, large: `NOT MY CONTEST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you've compared yourself to lately. Picture what they have that stings: the title, the house, the ease. Notice the old race starting in your chest. Now picture a starting line, and the race beginning without you. Stay where you are. Say inside: not my contest. Then name the contest that is yours today: being patient, being honest, finishing one thing well. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Not my contest. Epictetus' way to be unbeatable: enter no contest where winning isn't up to you, and envy has nowhere to stand. Today's word.
Your line: not my contest. Skip one comparison today. When it starts, say the line, and go back to your own race. Day three hundred fifty-one.

352.title: The insult
352.hook: it isn't the insulter who harms you but your judgment that you're harmed (Enchiridion 20)
352.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism pause, even for a single breath, before replying to an insult, giving the first flash of anger time to cool.

segments.voice: Yesterday: not my contest. That was also your line. Did you skip one comparison and go back to your own race? Day three hundred fifty-two.

A story told about Socrates in Diogenes Laertius' Lives of the Philosophers. A man in the street kicks him. His friends are outraged and want him to take the man to court. Socrates shrugs. If a donkey had kicked me, he asks, would I sue the donkey? We might not all manage that shrug. Somebody cuts in front at the pharmacy and calls you something under their breath, and for the rest of the afternoon you're writing speeches to them in your head. Section twenty of the handbook asks where, exactly, the injury happened. Today: the insult.
screen: `SOCRATES IS KICKED.` → `WOULD I SUE THE DONKEY?` → `WHERE DID THE INJURY HAPPEN?`

segments.voice: First, the claim. Remember, Epictetus says, that it isn't the one who abuses you or hits you who insults you. It's your judgment about them, that they've insulted you. The Greek verb is from hybris, outrage, the word behind our hubris. The outrage, he says, is completed inside. Second, the follow-through. So when someone provokes you, know that it's your own judgment that has provoked you. That sounds like blaming the victim, and it's worth slowing down here. Epictetus isn't saying the person behaved well, or that you shouldn't defend yourself or others from real harm. He's talking about the second injury, the one that keeps going all afternoon: the speeches in your head. That part, he says, runs on your verdict, and it can be looked at. Third, the tool. Try above all, he says, not to be carried off by the impression. If you once gain time and delay, you'll more easily master yourself. Time and delay. A breath. A count of three. Going to the window before answering the email. Fourth, an echo. Seneca, writing a whole essay on anger, said much the same: delay is the greatest remedy for anger. It's one of the places where the Stoic writers agree closely. The first flash is fast and hot. Many people find that if they give it a few seconds, it often cools enough for them to choose. So today's practice is small and exact. Not suppressing anything. Just putting one breath between the sting and the reply.
screen: `NOT THE INSULTER, BUT YOUR JUDGMENT.` · `THE SECOND INJURY.` · `GAIN TIME AND DELAY.` · `SENECA: DELAY IS THE REMEDY.` · then, large: `A BREATH BEFORE.`

segments.voice: Remember a moment when someone said something that stung. Let it replay, just once. Feel the heat rise, the reply forming. Now, at the exact point where you would answer, stop, and take one slow breath in and out. Only one. Notice what's different on the other side of it. Maybe the reply is the same. Maybe it's softer, or unnecessary. Then rest in the ordinary breathing that follows. The bell holds the time.
The insult. In Epictetus' handbook, completed not by the one who abuses you but by your judgment that you've been harmed, and loosened by a little delay. Today's word.
Your line: a breath before. Delay one reaction today by a single breath, the next time something stings. Then answer, if it still needs answering. Day three hundred fifty-two.

353.title: Nothing to envy
353.hook: keep death and exile before your eyes daily, and you won't grasp or envy (Enchiridion 21)
353.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners briefly bring death or loss to mind each day, as a way of loosening envy and grasping rather than as a source of fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the insult. Your line was a breath before. Did you put one breath between a sting and your reply? Day three hundred fifty-three.

When Epictetus wrote the word exile, he wasn't being abstract. His own teacher, Musonius Rufus, had been banished by Nero to a bare little island in the Aegean. Epictetus himself had to leave Rome when Domitian expelled the philosophers, and he rebuilt his life on another coast. Death wasn't abstract either: he had seen emperors kill senators for a sentence in a speech. So when section twenty-one tells us to keep death and exile before our eyes every day, it comes from someone who had lived beside both. And the payoff he promises is an odd one. Today: nothing to envy.
screen: `MUSONIUS, BANISHED TO AN ISLAND.` → `EPICTETUS, EXPELLED FROM ROME.` → `DEATH AND EXILE, DAILY.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. Let death and exile, and everything that seems terrible, be before your eyes every day, Epictetus says, and death most of all. Second, the promise. Then, he says, you'll never think anything low or petty, and you'll never want anything too much. Notice what he doesn't promise. Not that you'll be afraid less, at first, or cheerful. He promises a change in what you want. Third, how it works. Envy depends on a sense that the thing you envy is huge. Their promotion, their renovation, their perfect vacation. Set it in the light of death and it shrinks to its real size, not worthless, just the size of something that will be left behind. The Stoics weren't alone here. Many traditions keep a remembrance of death close: monks, mystics, poets. The Latin phrase memento mori, remember you'll die, came later, but the practice is old. Fourth, the gentle part. This isn't meant to darken the day. People who try it often report the opposite. The coffee tastes like coffee. The annoying coworker becomes a person who will also die, which is strangely tender. And envy, that tight, sour feeling, loosens, because in this light there's nothing to win. Everyone at the table, the one with the new car and the one with the old bike, is on the same short visit. Epictetus says it plainly: keep it before your eyes, and you won't grasp. If death feels too heavy today, start with exile: picture leaving behind everything you own. It does the same quiet work.
screen: `DEATH AND EXILE, BEFORE YOUR EYES.` · `NOTHING PETTY, NOTHING TOO MUCH.` · `ENVY SHRINKS TO ITS REAL SIZE.` · `THE SAME SHORT VISIT.` · then, large: `NOTHING TO ENVY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you envy. Someone's house, job, body, ease. See it clearly. Now gently widen the picture. Fifty years from now, or a hundred. The house belongs to strangers. The job is a line in a story nobody tells. The person is gone, and so are you. Hold it without fear, the way you'd look at the sea. Then look back at the thing you envied, and see what size it is now. The bell holds the time.
Nothing to envy. Epictetus' daily remembrance: keep death and exile before your eyes, and you'll want nothing too much and think nothing petty. Today's word.
Your line: nothing to envy. When envy pinches today, widen the picture for one breath, and let the thing shrink to its real size. Day three hundred fifty-three.

354.title: Expect to be laughed at
354.hook: take up philosophy and some will mock you; hold to what seems best (Enchiridion 22)
354.howItsDone: Many people who take up a philosophical or spiritual practice keep it quietly, without explaining or showing off, and let teasing pass.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nothing to envy. That was your line, too. When envy pinched, did you widen the picture and let it shrink? Day three hundred fifty-four.

You've been doing this practice for almost a year. Maybe you've started pausing before you answer. Maybe you sit for two minutes in the morning, or say a line under your breath at the stoplight. And maybe, at some point, someone noticed. A sibling rolled their eyes. A friend said, oh, so you're a philosopher now. A coworker caught you breathing at your desk and made a joke about it. Epictetus' students heard exactly the same jokes, almost word for word, two thousand years ago. He warned them before they went home. Today: expect to be laughed at.
screen: `ALMOST A YEAR OF PRACTICE.` → `OH, SO YOU'RE A PHILOSOPHER NOW.` → `THE SAME JOKES, TWO THOUSAND YEARS AGO.`

segments.voice: First, the warning. If you want philosophy, section twenty-two says, get ready from the start to be laughed at. Many will mock you. They'll say: he's come back to us a philosopher all of a sudden. And: where did he get that superior look? Second, the eyebrow. The Greek for that superior look is ophrys, literally the eyebrow, the raised brow of someone who thinks they're above it all. And here Epictetus turns to his own students first. Don't put on that look, he says. The mockers may be rude, but don't hand them a reason. Third, the holding. Instead, hold to what seems best to you, he says, as someone posted to that place by God. The image is a soldier at a post, not showing off, just staying. Readers who don't share Epictetus' belief in God can still hear the shape of it: a commitment you keep quietly, because it's yours to keep. Fourth, the two endings. If you stay with it, he says, the same people who laughed at first will come to admire you. But if you give in to them, you'll be laughed at twice. He might be too hopeful about the first. Some people never stop teasing. But the second rings true: dropping a practice because of a joke rarely ends the joking. It just adds a new one. So the advice comes down to this. No raised eyebrow. No speeches about your new morning routine. Just keep doing it, kindly, and let the laughter be weather.

segments.voice: Choose one small practice from this year that you want to keep. A pause, a line, a sit, a walk. Picture yourself doing it today, in front of whoever is most likely to tease you. Hear the joke. Notice the urge to explain, or to quit, or to look superior. Let all three go. See yourself just doing the practice, quietly, without a raised eyebrow, and then carrying on with your day. The bell holds the time.
Expect to be laughed at. Epictetus' warning to new students: some will mock, so don't put on airs, and hold to what seems best. Today's word.
screen: `EXPECT TO BE LAUGHED AT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: hold to it. Keep one practice quietly today, without announcing it, and if anyone laughs, smile and keep going. Day three hundred fifty-four.

355.title: Keep your footing
355.hook: turn outward to please someone and you've lost your footing (Enchiridion 23)
355.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners notice when they are shaping their words to win someone's approval, and return to saying what they actually think, kindly.

segments.voice: Yesterday: expect to be laughed at. Your line was hold to it. Did you keep a practice quietly, with no raised eyebrow? Day three hundred fifty-five.
screen: `EXPECT TO BE LAUGHED AT — HOLD TO IT.`

segments.voice: You're in a meeting and your manager floats an idea you think won't work. You open your mouth to say so. Then you see their face, hopeful, a little proud, and you hear yourself say: yeah, that could be great. Or you're at a party, and someone makes a joke about a group of people, and you laugh along, a beat late, because everyone else did. Afterward there's a small wobble, as if the floor had tilted. Section twenty-three of the handbook is two sentences long, and it names that wobble exactly. Today: keep your footing.
screen: `YEAH, THAT COULD BE GREAT.` → `LAUGHING A BEAT LATE.` → `THE FLOOR TILTS.`

segments.voice: First, the diagnosis. If it ever happens, Epictetus says, that you turn outward because you want to please someone, know that you've lost your footing. The Greek word is enstasis: a stance, a way of standing, a plan of life you've set yourself in. The moment you face outward to win approval, you've stepped off it. Second, what pleasing isn't. Kindness isn't the problem. Bringing a friend soup, choosing the restaurant your partner likes, laughing at a child's bad joke: those can all come from your own footing. The trouble is when the aim shifts from doing right to being liked, and you start bending your words to someone else's face. Third, the remedy. Be content, he says, in everything, simply to be a philosopher, a lover of wisdom. And if you also want to seem one, seem one to yourself. That's enough. It's a strangely freeing sentence. You need one witness, and you already have them. Fourth, the practice in real life. Keeping your footing doesn't mean saying every harsh thing you think. In the meeting, it might sound like: I'm not sure that will work, can I say why? At the party, it might be not laughing, and changing the subject. Quiet, small, honest. People-pleasing usually feels like it buys peace. Epictetus thinks the price is higher than it looks. Each time we tilt toward someone's approval, we hand them a little of the ground we stand on. Keep it.
screen: `TURNED OUTWARD TO PLEASE.` · `ENSTASIS: YOUR STANCE.` · `SEEM SO TO YOURSELF.` · `QUIET, SMALL, HONEST.` · then, large: `KEEP MY FOOTING.`

segments.voice: Stand up, if you can, or plant your feet flat on the floor where you sit. Feel your weight, even, on both feet. Now bring to mind a person you tend to bend toward: a boss, a parent, a friend whose approval you want. Picture them in front of you. Notice whether your body leans, even slightly. Come back to center. Feel both feet again. Picture saying one honest, kind sentence to them, from right here. The bell holds the time.
Keep your footing. Epictetus' warning: turn outward to please someone and you've stepped off your stance; be content to be what you are, in your own eyes. Today's word.
Your line: keep my footing. Skip one people-pleasing move today, the automatic yes, the late laugh, and say one honest, kind thing instead. Day three hundred fifty-five.

356.title: Faithful and modest
356.hook: you help your city not by holding office but by being trustworthy and self-respecting (Enchiridion 24)
356.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners measure their usefulness less by status or money than by being trustworthy and self-respecting in ordinary dealings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: keep your footing. Your line was keep my footing. Did you skip one automatic yes and say something honest and kind? Day three hundred fifty-six.

Every apartment building has one. The neighbor who signs for your packages and actually remembers to tell you. Who returns the ladder. Who says she'll water the plants while you're away, and you come home to plants that are alive. She doesn't sit on the city council. She'll never have a plaque. But the whole building runs a little better because she's in it. Some of Epictetus' students worried that a philosopher with no money and no office was useless to his friends and his city. Section twenty-four is his answer, and that neighbor is in it. Today: faithful and modest.
screen: `THE NEIGHBOR WHO SIGNS FOR PACKAGES.` → `NO OFFICE, NO PLAQUE.` → `IS A PHILOSOPHER USELESS?`

segments.voice: First, the worry. Don't let thoughts like this trouble you, Epictetus says: I'll live without honor, a nobody everywhere. Getting an office, being invited to the party, those aren't up to you. So how can missing them be your dishonor? You only need to be somebody in what's yours, and there you can be worth a great deal. Second, the friends. But my friends will get no help from me, the student says. What help? Epictetus asks. Money? Roman citizenship? Who told you those were in your power? Show me how to get them while staying trustworthy and self-respecting and generous, and I'll get them. But if you ask me to lose my own good so you can have things that aren't truly good, see how unfair that is. And what would you rather have, he asks: money, or a faithful, self-respecting friend? Third, the city. But my country will get no help from me. What help? It won't get colonnades or public baths from you. Fine. It doesn't get shoes from the blacksmith either, or weapons from the shoemaker. It's enough if each does their own work. If you made one more citizen trustworthy and self-respecting, would that be no use? Fourth, the two words. Faithful is pistos: trustworthy, the one whose word holds. Modest is aidemon: self-respecting, with a sense of shame in the good sense, the person who won't do what's beneath them. What place will you hold in the city, then? Whatever place you can hold while staying faithful and modest. Lose those trying to help, he says, and what use will you be, faithless and shameless? The neighbor with the ladder already knows this.
screen: `A NOBODY EVERYWHERE?` · `MONEY, OR A FAITHFUL FRIEND?` · `NO BATHS FROM YOU, AND THAT'S FINE.` · `PISTOS AND AIDEMON.` · then, large: `FAITHFUL AND MODEST.`

segments.voice: Think of one small promise you've made lately that's still open. Returning something. Answering a message. Showing up when you said. Picture the person waiting on it. Picture yourself keeping it today, simply, without fuss. Notice how small it is, and how much it says. Then let the words settle in you, slowly, with the breath: faithful, on the in breath; modest, on the out. The bell holds the time.
Faithful and modest. Epictetus' answer to feeling useless: trustworthy and self-respecting, you already serve your friends and your city. Today's word.
Your line: faithful and modest. Be reliable in one small thing today: keep the little promise you pictured, and don't mention it. Day three hundred fifty-six.

357.title: The price of lettuce
357.hook: someone else got invited: they paid the price in flattery, and you kept your coin (Enchiridion 25)
357.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners, when passed over, ask what price the other person paid and remind themselves of what they kept by not paying it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: faithful and modest. That was your line, too. Did you keep one small promise without mentioning it? Day three hundred fifty-seven, the end of a week.

The group photo goes up and you're not in it, because you weren't invited. Or the promotion goes to the person who laughs at all the boss's jokes and stays for every after-work drink. Or the dinner party is next Saturday and somehow your name didn't make the list. There's a sting, and right behind it, a question: why them and not me? Epictetus answers that question with a trip to the market. Specifically, to the vegetable stall, where a head of lettuce costs one small coin. Today: the price of lettuce.
screen: `THE PHOTO YOU'RE NOT IN.` → `WHY THEM AND NOT ME?` → `A TRIP TO THE MARKET.`

segments.voice: First, the situation. Someone was preferred to you, Epictetus says, at a dinner, or in being greeted, or in being asked for advice. If those are good things, be glad for them. If they're bad, don't be sorry they didn't come to you. Second, the market. How much is lettuce sold for? An obol, a small coin. Someone pays the obol and takes the lettuce. You don't pay, and you don't take it. Are you worse off than the buyer? He has the lettuce. You have the obol you didn't spend. Third, the real price. So it is here, he says. You weren't invited to someone's dinner? You didn't pay the host what the dinner sells for. And the price is praise, and attention, and hanging around his doors, and putting up with his rudeness. If it's worth it to you, pay the price and go. But if you want the dinner without paying, you're being greedy and foolish. Fourth, what you kept. And you haven't come away with nothing, he says. You have something in place of the dinner. You didn't praise someone you didn't want to praise. You didn't put up with their insolence at the door. That's the coin in your pocket. It doesn't mean every invitation is bought with flattery. Many are just friendship. But when someone gets ahead by paying a price you chose not to pay, Epictetus says: notice the coin you kept. And a look back at a week of steady footing: not my contest, the insult, nothing to envy, laughed at, keep your footing, faithful and modest, and the lettuce.
screen: `SOMEONE WAS PREFERRED TO YOU.` · `LETTUCE COSTS AN OBOL.` · `THE DINNER'S PRICE: PRAISE, ATTENTION.` · `THE COIN YOU KEPT.` · then, large: `I KEPT THE COIN.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing someone else got that you didn't. An invitation, a role, a compliment, a seat at a table. Let the sting come. Then ask Epictetus' market question: what did it cost?
